¶
'''tola<sup>1</sup>''' (tō′lä̤), ''n.'' [Hind. ''tola'', < Skt. ''tulā'', a balance, < √ ''tul'', lift up, weigh: see ''talent''<sup>1</sup>, ''tolerate''.] The fundamental unit of weight of the empire of India, by law precisely equal to 180 grains troy. It is about half a grain heavier than the old ''tola sicca''.

'''tola<sup>2</sup>''' (tō′lä̤), ''n.'' [Quichua.] In Peru, a native burial-mound.

{{smaller block|The only monuments of this neighborhood that escaped the fury of the conquerors are the ''tolas'' or mounds.
{{right|''Hassaurek'', Four Years among Spanish Americans, p. 318.}}}}

'''tolai''' (tō′lī), ''n.'' [Native name.] The Siberian hare, ''Lepus tolai''.

'''tolash†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''tolasshen''; < ''to-''<sup>2</sup> + ''lash''<sup>1</sup>.] To scourge severely.

{{smaller block|Goo ye and bete hym and all ''to-lasshe'' hym.
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 168.}}}}

'''tolbooth''', ''n.'' See ''tollbooth''.

'''told''' (tōld). Preterit and past participle of ''tell''<sup>1</sup>.

'''tole<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v.'' Same as ''toll''<sup>2</sup>, ''toll''<sup>3</sup>.

'''tole<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''tool''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Toledo''' (tọ̄-lē′dō), ''n.'' [So called from ''Toledo'' (< L. ''Toletum''), a city in Spain, long famous for manufacturing sword-blades of fine temper.] A sword-blade made, or supposed to be made, at Toledo in Spain, or a sword having such a blade; a Toledo blade or sword. {{smaller|Toledos were supposed to be of remarkably fine temper, and are said to have been of extraordinary elasticity.}}

{{smaller block|You sold me a rapier; . . . you said it was a ''toledo''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, iii. 1.}}}}

¶
'''toler''', ''n.'' See ''toller''<sup>2</sup>.

'''tolerability''' (tol″e̤-ra-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' [< ''tolerable'' + ''-ity'': see ''-bility''.] Tolerableness. ''Fuller.'' [Rare.]

'''tolerable''' (tol′e-ra-bl), ''a.'' [Formerly also ''tollerable''; < OF. ''tolerable'', F. ''tolérable'' = Pr. ''tollerable'' = Sp. ''tolerable'' = Pg. ''toleravel'' = It. ''tollerabile'', < L. ''tolerabilis'', that may be endured, < ''tolerare'', endure, tolerate see ''tolerate''.] 1. That may be borne or endured; supportable, either physically or mentally.

{{smaller block|It shall be more ''tolerable'' for the land of Sodom and Gomorrha in the day of judgment, than for that city.
{{right|Mat. x. 15.}}}}

2. Fit to be tolerated; sufferable.

{{smaller block|That langage that in the chambre is ''tollerable'' in place of iugement or great assembly is nothing commendable.
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, ii. 2.}}}}

3. Moderately good or agreeable; not contemptible; not very excellent or pleasing, but such as can be borne or received without positive approval or disapproval; passable; mediocre.

{{smaller block|The new front towards y<sup>e</sup> gardens is ''tollerable'', were it not drown'd by a too massie and clomsie pair of stayres of stone.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, June 9, 1658.}}
I only meant her to make a ''tolerable'' figure, without surpassing any one.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Daniel Deronda, x.}}}}

4. In fair health; passably well. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|We're ''tolerable'', sir, I thank you.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xxvi.}}}}

{{smaller block|The new front towards y<sup>e</sup> gardens is ''tollerable'', were it not drown'd by a too massie and clomsie pair of stayres of stone.

4. In fair health; passably well. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|We're ''tolerable'', sir, I thank you.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xxvi.}}}}

'''=Syn. 1''' and '''2.''' Endurable, bearable.—'''3.''' Indifferent, ordinary, so-so.

'''tolerableness''' (tol′e̤-ra̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being tolerable. ''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, II. 137.

'''tolerably''' (tol′e̤-ra̤-bli), ''adv.'' In a tolerable manner, in any sense.

'''tolerance''' (tol′e̤-ra̤ns), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''tollerance''; < OF. ''tolerance'', F. ''tolérance'' = Pr. ''toleransa'' = Sp. Pg. ''tolerancia'' = It. ''tolleranza'', < L. ''tolerantia'', endurance, < ''toleran(t-)s'', enduring, tolerant: see ''tolerant''.] 1. The state or character of being tolerant. {{smaller|(''a'') The power or capacity of enduring; the act of enduring; endurance: as, ''tolerance'' of heat or cold.}}

{{smaller block|Diogenes, one terrible frosty morning, came into the market-place, and stood naked, quaking, to shew his ''tolerance''.
{{right|''Bacon'', Works, I. 370.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b'') A disposition to be patient and indulgent toward those whose opinions or practices differ from one's own; freedom from bigotry or severity in judging of the opinions or conduct of others.}}

{{smaller block|The Christian spirit of charity and ''tolerance''.
{{right|''Bp. Horsley'', Sermons, II., App.}}}}

2. The act of tolerating; toleration.

{{smaller block|Remember that the responsibility of ''tolerance'' lies with those who have the wider vision.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, vii. 3.}}}}

3. In ''med.'', the power, either congenital or acquired, which an individual has of resistance to the action of a poison. Also ''toleration''.—4. In ''minting'', same as ''allowance''<sup>1</sup>, 7. See also ''remedy'', 4. Also ''toleration.''

{{smaller block|The limit of ''tolerance'' of the gold dollar being ¼ of a grain (nearly double the limit of abrasion), the gold dollar will continue current until reduced in weight below 25.55 grains.
{{right|''Report Sec. Treasury'', 1886, I. 271.}}}}

='''Syn. 1''' (''b''). Catholicity, liberality.—'''1''' (''b'') and '''2.''' ''Tolerance, Toleration.'' Generally ''tolerance'' refers to the spirit,

400 {{smaller block|and ''toleration'' to the conduct. One may show ''toleration'' from policy, without really having the spirit of ''tolerance.'' See ''tolerate.''}}

'''tolerant''' (tol′e̤-rant), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< OF. ''tolerant'', F. ''tolérant'' = Sp. Pg. ''tolerante'' = It. ''tollerante'', < L. ''toleran(t-)s'', ppr. of ''tolerare'', endure, tolerate: see ''tolerate.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Inclined or disposed to tolerate; favoring toleration; forbearing; enduring.

{{smaller block|The preface is evidently the work of a sensible and candid man, firm in his own religious opinions, and ''tolerant'' towards those of others.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Milton.}}}}

'''2.''' In ''med.'', able to receive or endure without effect, or without pernicious effect.

{{smaller block|The amount required to produce its effect [that of ipecacuanha] varies considerably, children as a rule being more ''tolerant'' than adults.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XIII. 210.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' One who tolerates; especially, one who is free from bigotry; a tolerationist.

{{smaller block|Henry the Fourth was a hero with Voltaire, for no better reason than that he was the first great ''tolerant.''
{{right|''J. Morley'', Voltaire, iii. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''tolerantly''' (tol′e̤-rant-li), ''adv.'' In a tolerant manner; with toleration.

'''tolerate''' (tol′e̤-rāt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''tolerated'', ppr. ''tolerating.'' [Formerly also ''tollerate''; < L. ''toleratus'', pp. of ''tolerare'' (> It. ''tollerare'' = Pg. Sp. ''tolerar'' = Pr. ''tollerar'' = OF. ''tolerer'', F. ''tolérer''), endure, tolerate, < √ ''tol'', in ''tollere'', bear, lift, ''tuli'', perf. of ''fero'', bear; cf. Gr. τλῆναι, suffer, Skt. √ ''tul'', lift, lift up, weigh, > ''tulā'', balance (see ''talent''<sup>1</sup>).] '''1.''' To sustain or endure; specifically, in ''med.'', to endure or support, as a strain or a drug, without pernicious effect.—'''2.''' To suffer to be or to be done without prohibition or hindrance; allow or permit negatively, by not preventing; put up with; endure; refrain from restraining; treat in a spirit of patience and forbearance; forbear to judge of or condemn with bigotry and severity: as, to ''tolerate'' opinions or practices.

{{smaller block|The Gospel commands us to ''tollerate'' one another, though of various opinions.
{{right|''Milton'', True Religion.}}}}

{{smaller block|They would soon see that criminal means once ''tolerated'' are soon preferred.
{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn.''' 2. ''Permit, Consent to'', etc. (see ''allow''<sup>1</sup>); brook, put up with, abide, bear, bear with.}}

¶
'''toleration''' (tol-e-rā′shon), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''tolleration''; < OF. ''toleration'', F. ''tolération'' = OSp. ''toleracion'' = It. ''tollerazione'', < L. ''toleratio(n-)'', < ''tolerare'', pp. ''toleratus'', endure, tolerate: see ''tolerate''.] 1†. The act of sustaining or enduring; endurance.

{{smaller block|There is also moderation in ''tolleration'' of fortune of euery sorte, whiche of Tullie is called equabilitie.
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 14.}}}}

2. The act of tolerating; allowance made for what is not wholly approved; forbearance.

{{smaller block|The indulgence and ''toleration'' granted to these men.
{{right|''South.''}}}}

'''3.''' Specifically, the recognition of the right of private judgment in matters of faith and worship; also, the liberty granted by the governing power of a state to every individual to hold or publicly teach and defend his religious opinions, and to worship whom, how, and when he pleases, provided that he does not thereby violate the rights of others or infringe laws designed for the protection of decency, morality, and good order, or for the security of the governing power; the effective recognition by the state of the right which every person has to enjoy the benefit of all the laws and of all social privileges without any regard to difference of religion.

{{smaller block|To this succeeded the King's declaration for an universal ''tolleration.''
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, March 12, 1672.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Toleration'' is of two kinds: the allowing to dissenters the unmolested profession and exercise of their religion, but with an exclusion from offices of trust and emolument in the state, which is a partial ''toleration''; and the admitting them without distinction to all the civil privileges and capacities of other citizens, which is a complete ''toleration.''
{{right|''Paley'', Elements of Political Knowledge, x.}}}}

'''4.''' A disposition to tolerate, or not to judge or deal harshly or rigorously in cases of differences of opinion, conduct, or the like; tolerance.—'''5.''' In ''med.'' and ''physiol.'', same as ''tolerance'', 3.

{{smaller block|Military surgery supplies many illustrations of ''toleration'' of shock and mildness of collapse after severe injuries to the medullary substance of the hemispheres.
{{right|''J. M. Carnochan'', Operative Surgery, p. 328.}}}}

'''6.''' Same as ''tolerance'', 4.

{{smaller block|In Germany and in the United States all silver coins, in France and Austria the major silver coins, are of the fineness 900, with a ''toleration'' of 3 units.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXII. 71.}}}}

'''7.''' A license to gather oysters or operate oyster-beds. The fee is a ''toleration fee.'' [Brookhaven, Long Island.]—'''Act of Toleration,''' in ''Eng. law,'' the name given to the statute 1 Will. and Mary (1689), cap. 18, by which Protestant dissenters from the Church of England, except such as denied the Trinity, on condition of taking the oaths of supremacy and allegiance, and repudiating the doctrine of transubstantiation, and, in the case of dissenting ministers, subscribing also to the Thirty-nine Articles, with certain exceptions relating to ceremonies, ordination, infant baptism, etc., were relieved from the restrictions under which they had formerly lain with regard to the exercise of religious worship according to their own forms. ='''Syn.''' See ''tolerance.''

'''tolerationist''' (tol-e̤-rā′shọn-ist), ''n.'' [< ''toleration'' + ''-ist.''] One who advocates toleration. ''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIV. 552.

'''tolerator''' (tol′e̤-rā-tọr), ''n.'' [< LL. ''tolerator'', one who endures, < L. ''tolerare'', endure, tolerate: see ''tolerate.''] One who tolerates. ''I. D'Israeli'', Curios. of Lit., IV. 139.

'''tolhouse†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''toll-house.''

'''tolibant†''' (tol′i-bant), ''n.'' Same as ''turban.''

'''toling''', ''n.'' See ''tolling''<sup>2</sup>.

'''tolipane†''', ''n.'' Same as ''turban.''

'''toll'''<sup>1</sup> (tōl), ''n.'' [< ME. ''tol'', ''tolle'', < AS. ''tol'', ''toll'' = OS. ''tolna'' = OFries. ''tolne'', ''tolene'', ''tolen'' = D. ''tol'' = MLG. ''toln'', ''tolen'', ''tollen'', ''tolne'', ''tolle'' = OHG. MHG. ''zol'', G. ''zoll'' = Icel. ''tollr'' = Sw. ''tull'' = Dan. ''told'' (Goth. not recorded), toll, duty, custom; orig. *''toln-'' (OS. ''tolna'', etc.) (''ln'' > ''ll'' by assimilation), lit. 'that which is counted or told,' from a strong pp. of the verb represented by the secondary weak form ''tell'', count, etc.: see ''tell'', and cf. ''tale''<sup>1</sup>, number, etc. Not connected with LL. ''telonium'', < Gr. τελώνιον, a custom-house, etc. (ML. ''toloneum'', ''tolonium'', ''tolnetum'', etc., toll, are perverted forms of ''telonium'', appar. simulating ''toll'').] A tax paid, or duty imposed, for some use or privilege or other reasonable consideration.

{{smaller block|Therfor ȝelde ȝe to alle men dettis, to whom tribut, tribut, to whom ''tol'', ''tol'' [custom, A. V.].
{{right|''Wyclif'', Rom. xiii. 7.}}}}

{{smaller block|Toulouse the riche,
I ȝif the . . .
The ''tolle'' and the tachementez, tavernez and other,
The towne and the tenementez with towrez so hye,
That towchez to the temperaltee, whilles my tyme lastez.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1568.}}}}

{{smaller block|The word ''toll'', in its earliest use, appears to have signified a franchise enjoyed by lords of manors, and is defined by Glanvill as the liberty of buying and selling in one's own land.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIII. 436.}}}}

{{smaller block|(''a'') The payment claimed by the owners of a port for goods landed or shipped there.}}

{{smaller block|Of wine, a ''toll'' in the strictest sense of the term was taken by the king's officer from every ship having in cargo ten casks or more, on the arrival of the ship at a port in England—viz., one cask from a cargo of ten up to twenty casks, and two casks from a cargo of twenty or more, unless the ''toll'' formed the subject of a composition in the way of a money payment.
{{right|''S. Dowell'', Taxes in England, I. 83.}}}}

{{smaller block|(''b'') The sum charged by the owners of a market or fair for goods brought to be sold there, or for liberty to break the soil for the purpose of erecting temporary structures. (''c'') A portion of grain retained by a miller as compensation for grinding. (''d'') A fixed charge made by those concerned in the maintenance of roads, streets, bridges, etc., for the passage, as at a toll-gate, of persons, goods, and cattle. (''e'') A compensation for services rendered, especially for transportation or transmission: as, canal ''tolls'', railway ''tolls'', and other charges have raised the price of wheat.}}

{{smaller block|As the expense of carriage is very much reduced by means of such public works, the goods, notwithstanding the ''toll'', come cheaper to the consumer than they would otherwise have done.
{{right|''Adam Smith'', Wealth of Nations, v. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|The estimate for special despatches includes telegraph ''tolls'' and pay of the correspondents who furnish the news.
{{right|''The Century'', XL. 260.}}}}

{{smaller block|'''Toll thorough,''' the toll taken by a town for persons, cattle, or goods going through it, or crossing a bridge or ferry maintained at its cost.}}

{{smaller block|''Toll thorough'' is paid for the use of a highway. In this case, if charged by a private person, some consideration, such as repair of the highway, must be shown, as such a toll is against common right. ''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIII. 436.}}

{{smaller block|'''Toll traverse,''' the toll exacted for passage or traffic over private land, bridges, ferries, etc.—'''Toll turne,''' or '''turn toll,''' a toll paid at the return of beasts from a fair or market where they were not sold.—'''To run toll,''' to avoid the payment of toll by running through the toll-gate. =''Syn.'' ''Duty'', ''Tribute'', etc. See ''tax''.}}

'''toll'''<sup>1</sup> (tōl), ''v.'' [< ME. ''tollen'' = Icel. ''tolla'' = Sw. ''tulla'' = Dan. ''tolde'', tax, take toll; from the noun.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' 1. To pay toll or tailage, as on a purchase.

{{smaller block|As ich leyue for the lawe asketh
Marchauns for here merchaundise in meny place to ''tollen''.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xiv. 51.}}}}

{{smaller block|I will buy me a son-in-law in a fair, and ''toll'' for this; I'll none of him. ''Shak.'', All's Well, v. 3. 149.}}

2. To take toll; exact or levy toll; especially, to take a portion of grain as compensation for grinding.

{{smaller block|Wel coude he stelen corn and ''tollen'' thryes.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 562.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
